reviews.title: The most unprofessional service from a lady in Bangalore
reviews.text:
I got assigned a lady called [name] in Bangalore for my service. After I got undressed, she pointed her phone towards me for a picture . I was  totally freaked out, I jumped out of the bed and she said she needs to upload pics for her company. Who takes pics after the person is undressed?? Even after that, she kept saying she’s connecting music etc.. I told her I will get into bed after she’s done with her work on the phone as I feel uncomfortable with a person having their phone while I’m undressed.. so she just said she doesn’t feel comfortable with me and is leaving. 

I had a really bad back ache and waited 45 mins for her to show up and she just cancelled . And the whole time I was soft spoken and polite with her, even the one second where the phone was pointed at me when she was taking my pic, I never helped I just jumped out of the camera frame. And just because I told her I want to get into bed after she’s finishes her phone stuff, she decided to leave

They should really have a way to file a complaint against such bad conduct and remove these providers from the app. After she left, I called the people and they just rescheduled a service. However, the previous provider disappeared from my app and I couldn’t even give her a rating or file a complaint against her. This means that whatever she is up to, she can go from house to house with her phone, and if anyone objects, she can just say I’m uncomfortable working with you and leave. And the people who are oblivious get taken for a ride. 

Honestly, my whole body is shaking after this experience even as a write this review. Definitely not using this app ever again

reviews.title: Extremely Disappointing First Experience – Painful Waxing, Skin Damage & Unprofessional Service
reviews.text:
This was my first booking with Yes Madam, and unfortunately, it turned out to be my worst salon experience. I booked my service for 7 PM, but the professional, [name], arrived in a hurry and seemed more interested in finishing the service quickly than providing proper care. Her approach was far from professional, and the entire experience felt no better than getting waxing done at a local parlour, despite booking through a professional service platform.

The waxing process was extremely harsh and painful, and my skin actually peeled off during the process. Even after 15 days, I still have a visible scar on my skin. This is completely unacceptable and raises serious concerns about the technique used, the care taken during the service, and the professional’s handling of sensitive skin.

My eyebrows were also not shaped properly and were left uneven, which was another disappointment.

What made the experience even worse was the handling of the products. The app clearly mentions that any remaining or unused products will be handed over to the customer. However, the professional did not use the Sokora scrub or lotion. When I asked about the scrub, she said that using it would cause my skin to peel. After waxing, she did not apply any lotion either. Despite not using these products, she refused to hand them over, saying that only the wax had been used.

This raises a genuine concern: if the products were not used, why were they not handed over as promised in the app? The service did not match the expectations set by the platform.

What I find particularly surprising is that this professional has a 4.8 rating on Yes Madam. After such a painful and disappointing experience, I genuinely question how accurately the ratings and reviews reflect the quality of service customers actually receive. I cannot say whether the reviews are genuine, but my personal experience was completely inconsistent with the rating.

A professional beauty service should prioritise hygiene, proper technique, customer comfort, and skin safety—not rush through a booking. I paid for a professional service and ended up with an uneven eyebrow shape, an extremely painful waxing experience, and a scar that is still visible after 15 days.

I would not recommend Yes Madam based on this experience. My first booking has left me extremely disappointed, and I have lost confidence in the quality control of the platform. I hope Yes Madam takes customer complaints seriously, investigates such incidents, and ensures that its professionals follow proper procedures and the product-handling policy mentioned in the app.

Instead of acknowledging the issue with the app, the expert repeatedly blamed me for the incorrect location. I had not selected that location myself, so it was extremely frustrating to be made responsible for something I had no control over.

Once she arrived, she decided the sequence of services herself. She started with waxing and then proceeded with the pedicure. By the time the pedicure was completed, she was already in a rush. As a result, one of my booked services — threading — was completely missed.

She also left the garbage packet behind without informing me. When I asked what I was supposed to do with it, she told me that I was supposed to throw it away. This has never been my experience with Yes Madam earlier. Previously, experts either asked me how the waste should be disposed of or disposed of it themselves in the dustbin that was already available in the bathroom.

Another issue was the leftover product. When I asked for the leftover product, I was told that it would only be handed over if I had booked both manicure and pedicure, and otherwise she was not supposed to give it to me. This was confusing because Yes Madam promotes its products as being exclusively for the service and single-use. If the product is genuinely meant for one-time use, I fail to understand why the leftover product was simply taken away instead of being handled transparently.

The most disappointing part was that the expert left without completing the service. She was asking for the OTP while leaving, and I was so confused by the rush that I didn’t immediately realise that threading had been missed. I called her 3–4 times immediately afterwards, but she did not answer. I even contacted my society’s guard room and was told that she had not yet left the society. Despite being there, she did not respond to my calls.

I subsequently contacted customer care and explained the entire situation. I expected them to arrange the missed service, even if it had to be done later that day or the next day. I was flexible about the timing. Instead, I was told that the amount would be credited to my Yes Madam wallet/cash balance, which could only be used when I booked another service worth ₹500 or more.

This was extremely disappointing. I had paid for a service that was not completed, and instead of arranging the pending service or providing an appropriate resolution, I was essentially told to spend more money with the company in order to use the amount I had already paid.

What disappointed me most was the complete lack of accountability. The location issue was blamed on me. The missed service was effectively my responsibility because I apparently should have remembered everything that had to be done. The expert’s rush and incomplete service were not adequately addressed. And customer care did not provide a meaningful solution either.

As a customer, I should not have to manage the expert’s timing, remind her about the services I have already booked, ensure that she doesn’t leave before completing them, and then chase her after she leaves.

I have used Yes Madam services before and had much better experiences, which is why this experience was particularly disappointing. This time, it felt as though the priority was simply to complete the payment and close the booking rather than actually ensure that the customer received the service that was paid for.

I hope Yes Madam seriously reviews this incident, the expert’s conduct, the handling of the booking/location issue, and the customer-care resolution process. A customer should not be made responsible for problems caused by the app, nor should they have to bear the loss when a booked service is left incomplete.

However, repeated service failures, poor communication, lack of accountability, and disrespectful customer handling cannot continue.

story.t1: 59% of complaints come down to three things: no-shows and cancellations, price and offer clarity and service quality.
story.t2: No-shows and cancellations lead, at 20% of complaints. Customers don't just dislike them; many have already called support about them.
story.t3: Each driver traces back to something the operation does, not something customers do.
story.t4: The top three drivers are the bulk of the support load, and the bigger cost is customers who don't come back.
story.t5: Three fixes, three owners, one metric each: contacts per 100 bookings by driver.
story.tR: Why customers contact Yes Madam, and what to fix first.
story.tB: Same top drivers as Urban Company, but Yes Madam over-indexes on products.
story.tC: Complaints by month and by app version.
story.paretoNote: 72 complaints (25%) say they already contacted support, and 63 of them say support didn't fix it. Weighted by who already called, the top three are 71% of contacts, and no-shows and cancellations alone are 36%.

whys.problem: Bookings fail at or after the slot time, and the customer is the last to know.

chain.text: The assigned professional declined, went on leave or fell ill, and no one else was sent (#62, #247, #250).
Nobody checks before the slot that she is coming. The customer finds out at the slot time, or only when she calls support (#15, #193, #338).
Accepting a job does not lock the professional in. Some ask the customer to cancel instead, so the drop is logged as a customer cancellation (#127, #219, #362).
The app shows slots when no professional is free, and products run short too, so there is no one ready to send instead (#73, #284, #394).
Slots are sold off the calendar, not off confirmed professional capacity in that area and hour, and payment is taken before anyone confirms.

whys.root: Slots are sold before a professional is confirmed, and nothing checks or backfills a dropped job before the slot time.
whys.test: If most failed bookings had a professional confirmed 2 hours before the slot and still failed, the problem is on-the-day behaviour, not slot inventory.

whys.problem: Customers feel tricked: the free offer is gone in a minute, and the price grows at checkout.

chain.text: The offer they were sent could not be booked, or the final price was higher than the price shown (#10, #23).
The free pedicure opens at 1 pm for everyone. Slots are gone by 1:02, and the app crashes at checkout in the rush (#78, #121, #138).
It reads as a scam, not a sell-out, because it is pushed to everyone without saying how many slots exist (#48, #77).
Compulsory fees sit outside the listed price: a platform fee, a ₹99 kit charge, a ₹300 line labelled tax. They appear only at checkout (#55, #126, #190).
Offers and price pages are judged on installs and visits, not on how many offers are honoured or how many complaints they create.

whys.root: Offers and prices are built to attract, not to be honoured: a tiny flash offer pushed to everyone, and compulsory fees shown only at checkout.
whys.test: If offer complaints spike only on days the app crashed at 1 pm, this is an engineering capacity problem, not offer design.

whys.problem: The service itself goes wrong: untrained or rushed work, rude behaviour, and burns or rashes (11 of the 24 burn or reaction reviews follow waxing).

chain.text: The professional lacked the skill for that service: burnt skin after waxing, ruined brows, half-done work (#41, #152, #191).
Professionals reach customers before their skill on each service is proven. Quality is checked by ratings after the job, not before it.
Professionals rush the job ('in too much hurry', a facial done in 30 minutes), likely because back-to-back slots leave no slack (#50, #264, #351).
When something goes wrong, the answer is a coupon, not a call-back or care for the injury: a ₹400 coupon for a burnt hand (#41, #104, #217).
Complaints are closed case by case in support and don't flow back to the professional's record, training or assignment.

whys.root: No closed loop from complaint to professional: skill isn't certified per service before risky jobs like waxing, and complaints end in coupons instead of retraining.
whys.test: If complaints are spread evenly across professionals rather than concentrated in a few, the problem is training content or products, not specific people.

fixes.name: Confirm or reassign 2 hours before
fixes.what: Professional confirms 2 hours before the slot. No confirmation means auto-reassign from the nearby pool, and the customer gets a message with a choice before the slot, not after. Sell slots only against confirmed capacity. Log a professional's 'please cancel' as a partner cancellation.
fixes.target: Down 40% in 8 weeks; 90% of failures with 2+ hours' notice
fixes.measure: Pilot in 2 cities against 2 similar cities for 4 weeks. Track failed bookings, notice given, reassign success, and contacts per 100 bookings for 'where is my professional'.

fixes.name: Price shown is price paid; honest offers
fixes.what: Show compulsory fees inside the listed price. Label flash offers with the number of slots ('200 free pedicures today') and give a waitlist or coupon when they run out. Load-test the 1 pm checkout.
fixes.metric: Offer and price complaints per 1,000 bookings
fixes.target: Down 50%, with checkout conversion flat or better
fixes.measure: A/B test all-in prices on 10% of users for 2 weeks: conversion, cart-to-payment drop-off, and contacts tagged offer or charges. Track app crashes in the 1 pm window.

fixes.name: Certify risky services; close the loop on complaints
fixes.what: Certify each professional per service, waxing first, before she is assigned it. Every injury complaint gets a call within 24 hours, care for the customer, and the professional is paused and retrained. Weekly list of professionals with 2+ complaints.
fixes.metric: Injury and quality complaints per 1,000 jobs
fixes.target: Down 30% in 12 weeks; no repeat complaint within 30 days of retraining
fixes.measure: Before and after by hub cohort. Check how concentrated complaints are: if the worst 10% of professionals carry most of them, target them first.

plan30: Week 1: pull the last 90 days of support tickets and tag them with this codebook. Compare the ticket mix with this review mix.
Week 2: put rupees on each driver from real data: contacts, refunds, compensation coupons and lost repeat bookings.
Week 3: start the two pilots: confirm-or-reassign in 2 cities, and all-in prices for 10% of users.
Week 4: first readout to you, and a weekly contacts-per-100-bookings view by driver.
story.northStarNote: It falls only if customers have fewer reasons to call, which is the point. Watch first-contact resolution next to it, so contacts aren't cut by making support harder to reach.

root: Slots are sold before a professional is confirmed, and nothing checks or backfills a dropped job before the slot time.
Offers and prices are built to attract, not to be honoured: a tiny flash offer pushed to everyone, and compulsory fees shown only at checkout.
No closed loop from complaint to professional: skill isn't certified per service before risky jobs like waxing, and complaints end in coupons instead of retraining.
impact: At about 3.5 lakh bookings a month and an assumed 12 contacts per 100 bookings, that is about 42,000 contacts a month.
The top three drivers would be about 59% of them, about 24,800 a month. A 30% cut removes about 7,400 contacts a month, or ₹40.2 L a year at ₹45 a contact.
The bigger prize is retention: if 1 in 10 customers behind those bad experiences would otherwise leave, keeping them is worth up to ₹4.8 Cr a year at ₹5,400 a customer.
action: Confirm or reassign 2 hours before: failed bookings per 100, partner side, down 40% in 8 weeks; 90% of failures with 2+ hours' notice.
Price shown is price paid; honest offers: offer and price complaints per 1,000 bookings, down 50%, with checkout conversion flat or better.
Certify risky services; close the loop on complaints: injury and quality complaints per 1,000 jobs, down 30% in 12 weeks; no repeat complaint within 30 days of retraining.

One offer campaign can flood reviews for weeks. Check the month view before calling it structural.
Most contacts never become reviews, and quick 'where is my professional' calls rarely do. The ticket mix will differ.
Claims such as theft or injury are allegations, not verified facts. They are counted, not judged.
